stories.title: Two Dead, Twelve Missing as Migrant Boat Capsizes Off Tunisian Coast
stories.summary:
A migrant boat capsized off the coast of southern Tunisia, resulting in a significant loss of life and missing persons. The incident occurred while the vessel was reportedly heading toward Italy.

Tunisia's national guard initially reported that at least two people were killed and 12 others remained missing following the capsize. One survivor was rescued from the water.

Subsequent reporting by Al Jazeera indicated a higher death toll, stating that eight of the 15 Tunisian nationals on board died when the boat sank off the southeastern coast. The discrepancy in casualty figures highlights the evolving nature of the initial emergency response.

The tragedy has sparked public reaction within Tunisia, with protests emerging in the wake of the sinking. The incident underscores the ongoing dangers faced by migrants attempting to cross the Mediterranean Sea.

links.excerpt: A migrant boat carrying 15 Tunisians sank off the country's southeastern coast while heading to Italy, killing eight.

stories.title: Landfill collapse in Guinea kills at least 30 people
stories.summary:
A landfill collapse in Guinea has killed at least 30 people after heavy rains triggered a landslide. The disaster occurred at a major waste site in the capital, where a mound of rubbish buried several homes and shacks.

The government confirmed that the collapse happened when rainwater washed over the site, causing the unstable pile to give way. Rescue efforts are ongoing as authorities assess the full extent of the damage.

stories.title: Karmelo Anthony denied motion for retrial after murder conviction
stories.summary:
A Texas judge has denied Karmelo Anthony's motion for a retrial following his murder conviction. The decision was made on Saturday after a two-day court hearing.

Anthony, a 19-year-old Black man, was convicted of fatally stabbing Austin Metcalf, a 17-year-old white athlete, at a high school track meet in Texas. He was sentenced to 35 years in prison for the crime.

Judge Michael Chitty rejected the defense's bid for a new trial, leaving the original conviction and sentence intact. The denial comes two months after Anthony was found guilty of murder.

stories.title: Accused Drug Trafficker Leaves Post as Mexican Governor, One Day After Resuming Office
stories.summary:
Rubén Rocha Moya, the governor of Mexico's Sinaloa state who faces U.S. drug trafficking charges, announced he is stepping down indefinitely from his post.

The abrupt decision came just over a day after he had resumed his duties following a period of leave.

His return to office triggered significant internal conflict within Mexico's ruling MORENA party.

President Claudia Sheinbaum and other state governors publicly distanced themselves from Rocha Moya, criticizing him for prioritizing personal interests over the well-being of the nation and the party.

stories.title: Seven First Nations Australians tell us their worries and hopes for future generations – video
stories.summary:
Seven First Nations Australians share their worries and hopes for future generations in a new video from The Guardian Australia.

The piece highlights East Arnhem Land, described as one of the last strongholds of Aboriginal culture in Australia. It is home to the Yolngu people, who maintain one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth.

The land is fully owned and managed by traditional owners under inalienable Aboriginal freehold title, meaning it can never be bought or sold.

Each year, the Yolngu host the Garma festival, described as Australia's largest Indigenous political and cultural gathering. The event brings together First Nations leaders from around the country.

stories.title: Is it legal to train AI models on copyrighted books? It’s complicated
stories.summary:
The legality of training artificial intelligence models on copyrighted books remains a complex and unsettled issue. Many published authors have unknowingly contributed to the development of AI tools that now threaten their livelihoods, raising questions about whether such practices are inherently illegal.

While the use of copyrighted material without knowledge or consent appears problematic, the legal landscape is not straightforward. The situation involves nuanced interpretations of copyright law and fair use, making it difficult to draw a simple conclusion about the permissibility of these AI training methods.

stories.title: If all car tyres were filled with CO2, would this cut atmospheric carbon significantly?
stories.summary:
A recent Guardian Q&A explores whether filling all car tires with carbon dioxide could meaningfully reduce atmospheric carbon. The question taps into broader concerns about consumerism and the climate emergency.

The idea suggests that using CO2 as a tire filler might lock away enough carbon to make a difference. However, the scale of global vehicle fleets is vast, and the amount of gas required would be enormous.

While the concept is intriguing, experts generally view it as impractical for large-scale climate mitigation. The primary challenge remains reducing emissions at their source rather than relying on unconventional storage methods.

stories.title: Will AI give you the job? Automated hiring tools spark discrimination and secrecy lawsuits
stories.summary:
A growing number of lawsuits are challenging the use of artificial intelligence in employment decisions, raising fresh questions about how companies hire and fire. The legal disputes center on automated hiring tools that applicants say have contributed to discrimination and opaque decision-making.

The Guardian reports that Erin Kistler, a product manager with nearly four years of job applications behind her, has sent thousands of résumés to major employers including PayPal, Microsoft, and Netflix. Despite her experience, she describes the process as sending her qualifications into a “black hole,” highlighting the frustration many applicants face when their applications are filtered by algorithms rather than human review.

These cases reflect broader concerns about secrecy in AI-driven recruitment systems. As companies increasingly rely on automation to screen candidates, plaintiffs argue that the lack of transparency makes it difficult to determine whether biased or flawed models are influencing hiring outcomes.

stories.summary:
Facial recognition technology at major Australian supermarkets has drawn criticism over privacy concerns. Coles and Woolworths say they are exploring the technology to improve safety, but experts warn it could normalize surveillance in everyday shopping environments.

The debate highlights a tension between retail security measures and customer privacy rights. Critics argue that widespread use of facial recognition in stores may set a precedent for broader monitoring without adequate safeguards or public consent.
